articles.title: Playwright connect_over_cdp Hangs 100s? Check for One Dead Tab
articles.excerpt: If connect_over_cdp hangs for 100 seconds while /json/version answers instantly, Chrome is not dead. One open tab has a hung renderer, and Playwright's auto-attach is waiting on it. Find that tab over…
articles.body: If connect_over_cdp hangs for 100 seconds while /json/version answers instantly, Chrome is not dead. One open tab has a hung renderer, and Playwright's auto-attach is waiting on it. Find that tab over a raw browser-level websocket, close only that tab, and connect again. Do not restart Chrome. I got this wrong the first time. The write-up of the original incident is in this post on my blog ; this is the version for people who just want the diagnosis and the commands. The symptom: a 100-second hang with a healthy endpoint Chrome was running with its debugging port on 9401. My script did the usual thing: from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright CDP = " http://127.0.0.1:9401 " with sync_playwright () as p : b = p . chromium .

So I built World 001: my story as a painted London you can walk through on chaseintech.com . What it is World 001 is a single, depth-mapped painting of London at dusk. The camera drifts across it with real parallax. Hover anywhere and places light up. Click one and the camera flies you to that stop, where a short card tells that part of the story in my own words. There are ten stops, from the boxing ring and the run club to the reselling shelves, the lecture halls and the glass house where I build AI agents. It ends at first light. It runs in the browser on desktop and phone, with no app to install.

articles.title: Pasting .env into Claude Code? Give the agent one dotvault service token instead
articles.excerpt: This is part 8 of the series "dotvault, Start to Finish: One Command from Your Laptop to CI, Your Team, and Your AI Agents." dotvault will be released free of charge when this series ends. I gave Clau…
articles.body: This is part 8 of the series "dotvault, Start to Finish: One Command from Your Laptop to CI, Your Team, and Your AI Agents." dotvault will be released free of charge when this series ends. I gave Claude Code exactly one thing: a dotvault service token, limited to one project and one environment. No .env in the chat, no email and password. It ran dotvault init , import , pull , run and whoami on its own, imported 3 keys and pulled the same 3 back, then wrote me a report of what it had done. When I revoked the token in the console and asked for the same pull again, it failed with AUTH_REQUIRED and exit code 3, and Claude Code told me so. This is part 8 of 12 in a series on dotvault, which keeps .env secrets for a team and hands them to people, CI and AI agents.

articles.body: Book: System Design Pocket Guide: Interviews Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub Your mobile app reads total_cents from GET /orders/{id} . After this branch lands, that field is gone. The agent renamed it to totalCents "for consistency", regenerated openapi.yaml and updated the handler and its tests, so the suite is green. The app lives in another repository, so the server's tests can't fail on its behalf. And the agent rewrote those tests along with the code. Nothing in this repo knows the client exists. The spec does, though. On main , total_cents is a required field of the response.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 6, 1572: A German astronomer discovers the Tycho supernova with the naked eye, but everyone thought the cosmic explosion was a 'new star'
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova later caleld the Tycho supernova with his bare eyes. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 6, 1572, the German astronomer Wolfgang Schulër observed a supernova with his bare eyes. He spotted the exploding star in the constellation Cassiopeia. It was as bright as Venus and could even be seen during the day. Astronomers were really confused, because it looked like a star just appeared out of nowhere. Schulër may have been the first to see it, but the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe is widely credited for the discovery. Brahe studied it in detail and wrote a whole book about this so-called "new star." It then became known as "Tycho's Star." At the time, supernovas had not yet been discovered. Tycho's Star was finally classified as a supernova in the 1940s. Scientists now think it was a small star called a white dwarf that exploded thousands of years ago.

articles.body: Early morning risers heading to work or school before sunrise are likely to notice a very bright, star-like object appearing low in the east-southeast sky just before sunrise. What is somewhat amazing is that just a couple of weeks ago this object wasn't there at all, but now it literally stands out with such brilliance as to almost command the attention of commuters who might be traveling in an easterly direction to "Look at me!" The object in question is, of course, the planet Venus, which is currently amid one of its most spectacular forays into the morning sky, literally "vaulting up" into prominence. On Oct. 24, Venus came to inferior conjunction, passing between the Earth and sun and shifting from the evening into the morning sky.

articles.title: I finally got my hands on the Unistellar Envision smart binoculars with augmented reality and I can’t wait to stargaze with them
articles.excerpt: The Unistellar Envision smart binoculars have an augmented reality (AR) overlay that provides smart functionality to 10x50 binoculars, enabling night sky and landmark identification.
articles.body: I have been waiting to get my hands on a pair of Unistellar Envision smart binoculars since they were announced in 2024. Our editor-in-chief tried an early demo of them last year and said that they felt like something out of Star Trek . He was, of course, referencing the red augmented reality (AR) overlay in the Envisions that can identify night sky targets and landmarks, as well as displaying navigational tools. These are the first pair of smart binoculars that can identify targets in the night sky, such as planets, stars and deep space objects. The build is solid and while they aren't the most lightweight binoculars , the body is hiding that extra technology that enables the AR overlay in the right hand lens.

articles.title: See the space race like you’ve never seen it before in PBS’s new living documentary, ‘We Chose to Go to the Moon’
articles.excerpt: Hear Neil Armstrong's son and granddaughter sing a moving tribute to the legendary Apollo 11 astronaut
articles.body: Straight from its inspiring live performance at New York City's Carnegie Hall this past April, RadicalMedia's filmed presentation of the immersive living space documentary, "We Chose to Go to the Moon," is finally available for the rest of us to watch. "We Chose to Go to the Moon" premieres Nov. 10 at 8:00 p.m. ET on PBS, PBS.org, and the PBS app, and we’ve got an exclusive clip to share featuring Mark and Kali Armstrong singing "Flight of Fancy." With a poignant introduction by Oscar winning director Ron Howard ("Apollo 13"), "We Chose to Go to the Moon" recalls the extraordinary saga of the global space race and Apollo moon landings by actors portraying pivotal persons who made it all happen.

articles.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
articles.excerpt: The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.
articles.body: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened.
